title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
hook: Carbon monoxide is invisible and odorless. A working alarm is the only thing that will warn you before it's too late.
key_points: Put smoke alarms on every level, inside each bedroom, and outside sleeping areas.
Install CO alarms on every level and near sleeping areas.
Test alarms monthly and replace batteries when they chirp.
Replace smoke alarms about every 10 years; CO alarms per the maker's date.
If a CO alarm sounds, get everyone to fresh air and call for help.
content_html: Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are cheap, but a working one is among the most life-saving things in a home. Carbon monoxide (CO) is especially dangerous because it's invisible and has no smell, so an alarm is your only early warning.
extra_html:
The CDC recommends installing CO alarms on every level of the home and near sleeping areas. Smoke alarm guidance is similar: one on every level, inside each bedroom, and outside each sleeping area. Test all alarms monthly using the test button, and replace batteries promptly when an alarm chirps to signal a low battery.

Alarms don't last forever. Smoke alarms generally need replacing about every 10 years, and CO alarms according to the manufacturer's date on the unit. The CDC also stresses prevention: never run a generator, grill, or car engine in an enclosed space. If a CO alarm sounds, move everyone to fresh air right away and call for help, then don't go back inside until it's cleared.

source.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

related.hook: Most poisonings happen at home with everyday products. How you store them is your first line of defense.

related.title: How Extreme Heat Harms the Body
related.hook: Your body cools itself by sweating — but in high heat and humidity, that system can be overwhelmed, and the result can be deadly. Knowing the signs is how you stay ahead of it.

flashcards.prompt: Why do homes need carbon monoxide alarms specifically?
flashcards.back_html: Carbon monoxide is a gas you cannot see or smell, so you won't notice dangerous levels building up. A CO alarm is the only reliable way to be warned in time.

flashcards.prompt: What should you do first if your carbon monoxide alarm goes off?

choices.text: Get everyone outside to fresh air and call for help
Open one window and go back to sleep
Wait to see if the alarm stops on its own

flashcards.explanation_html: Because CO can be deadly fast, the priority is getting everyone out to fresh air immediately and then calling for help.
